title: Railway Time
sub: Grades 5–8 · Math · Elapsed time, offsets and rate
objective: Before the railways, every town in Britain set its clocks by the Sun, so the further west, the later its clocks. Students will use the 1841 Great Western Railway timetable’s minutes — how far each town’s time was behind London’s — to convert between a town’s own time and the London time the trains ran by, solve elapsed-time problems that cross the hour, and treat each town as a signed offset. Red Level students will find a rate, minutes per degree west, and use it to test the timetable.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Every clock in the world is still set by the same reasoning: a time, an offset, and a rule for turning one into the other. Time zones are railway time on a bigger map.

materials: The timetable and answer key on page 3, projected or printed; the handouts, one per student
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** at the railway bench of the *Inventions Workshop,* drag the Sun west across the map, steam down the line comparing your watch with each town clock, catch the train, wind on the station clocks, and set Bristol’s two-handed clock.

steps.title: Two right times
script: Ask: *“A traveler’s watch says 12:00 noon. Bristol’s clock says 11:49. Can they both be right?”* Take ideas. Then tell students that in Victorian Britain both could be right: towns kept their own time by the Sun, and noon came later the further west you went. Bristol’s time was 11 minutes behind London’s.

screen.question: A traveler’s watch says 12:00 noon. Bristol’s clock says 11:49. Can they both be right?

steps.purpose: Meet the puzzle of two correct times before the rule is given.
students: How could two clocks both be right?

steps.title: Minutes behind London
script: **The timetable.** In 1841 the Great Western Railway’s timetable read *“LONDON TIME is kept at all the Stations on the Railway,”* and gave how many minutes each town’s time was behind it: Reading 4, Steventon 5½, Chippenham 8, Bath 11, Bristol 11, Bridgewater 14. Show the number line.

**The rule.** A town’s clock is *behind*, so to find London time, count on: **London time = town time + minutes behind.** Work Bath together: its clock says 11:52, plus 11 minutes is 12:03 London time, and the 12:00 train has gone. A traveler who forgot that London time was ahead risked missing the train.

line.alt: A number line of minutes behind London time, from 0 to 18: London at 0, Reading 4, Chippenham 8, Bath and Bristol 11, Bridgewater 14, and Plymouth 16 and a half, behind Greenwich.

worked.title: Will you catch the train at Bath?
steps: The train leaves at **12:00 noon, London time**.
Bath’s own clock says **11:52**. Bath is **11 minutes behind** London.
Count on 11 minutes to find London time: **11:52 + 0:11 = 12:03**.

screen.rule:
London time = town time + minutes behind
Town time = London time − minutes behind

steps.purpose: Learn the rule for turning a town’s time into London time, and back.
students: When London says 12:00 noon, what does Reading’s clock say?
Why do the clocks get later going west?

steps.title: Wind the clocks on
script: **The other way.** The stationmaster’s clock must say London time. If the telegraph brings 12:10 and Reading’s clock shows 12:06, wind it on 4 minutes. Bristol’s Exchange clock solved the problem with two minute hands: a red one for London time and a black one for Bristol’s own.
**Offsets.** Write each town as a signed number: London 0, Reading −4, Bath −11. The difference between two towns is the distance between their numbers: from Reading to Bath is 11 − 4 = 7 minutes.

examples.title: You’re the stationmaster
steps: Reading’s clock still shows Reading’s own time, 4 minutes behind: **12:06**.

examples.title: Bristol’s clock with two minute hands
steps: The red hand shows London time: **12:10**.
The black hand shows Bristol’s own time, 11 minutes behind: **11:59**.
The train leaves at **12:30 London time**. What will the black hand show?

steps.purpose: Practice both directions of the rule: a clock to wind on, and a clock with two hands.
students: How far must Bath’s clock be wound on?
Why did Bristol need two minute hands?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three use the timetable’s minutes; the train times and the 12:10 telegraph are the workshop’s game.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Read the timetable; convert London noon to town time; decide two train puzzles with a frame; wind on two station clocks.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Solve all four train puzzles; do the stationmaster’s job for four towns; use Bristol’s two-handed clock; compare towns with signed offsets.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Plot minutes behind against degrees west, find the rate, check it against Earth’s turning, and judge which timetable figures fit; find the angle between two minute hands.

steps.purpose: Convert, compare and test railway time at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. Show the minutes you add or take away.

steps.title: The four trains
script: Project the chart and reveal the four trains one by one. Ask a Red Level student: *what pattern did the data show, and which figures did not fit it?* Then ask why one standard time for the whole country made railway timetables easier.
